rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Thermal conduction transfers heat without material motion. Fourier's law: dQ/dt = kAΔT/d. Thermal resistance R = d/(kA); series resistances add. Metals conduct well (free electrons); insulators poorly. Steady-state, one-dimensional flow assumed.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Fourier's law: dQ/dt = kAΔT/d
Heat current: H = ΔT/R where R = d/(kA)
Series resistance: R_total = Σ dᵢ/(kᵢA)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Steady State: Fourier's law applies in steady state (temperature at each point constant in time). Transient state requires heat equation.  ·  One-Dimensional: Heat flow perpendicular to slab faces, no heat loss from sides (insulated).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Statement 1: Rate of heat conduction through a slab: dQ/dt = kAΔT/d.  ·  Statement 2: Thermal conductivity k is a material property (W/(m·K)).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Confusing thermal conductivity k with heat capacity: k measures heat transfer rate; heat capacity measures heat needed to raise temperature.  ·  Thinking temperature drop is equal across series slabs: ΔTᵢ = H·Rᵢ — larger drop across larger resistance.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Thermal Conduction: Heat transfer through a material without bulk motion of the material. Energy passes from particle to particle via molecular collisions and free electron movement (in metals).  ·  Rate of Heat Flow: For steady-state conduction through a slab of area A, thickness d, thermal conductivity k, temperature difference ΔT: dQ/dt = kAΔT/d = kA(T₁ - T₂)/d. This is Fourier's law of heat conduction.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: H = kAΔT/d — remember H = ΔT/R form too.  ·  Series slabs: same H through each; total R = R₁ + R₂ + ...

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. State Fourier's law of heat conduction and define thermal conductivity.  ·  Q2. Derive dQ/dt = kAΔT/d for steady-state conduction.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: NEB frequently asks for Fourier's law derivation and numericals on composite slabs.  ·  Calculate interface temperature in series slabs.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Conduction: heat transfer without material motion.  ·  dQ/dt = kAΔT/d — Fourier's law of heat conduction.  ·  k is material property; metals high, insulators low.  ·  Thermal resistance R = d/(kA); series: R_total = ΣRᵢ.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Diamond has highest thermal conductivity (~2000 W/(m·K)) — used in high-power electronics cooling.  ·  Air is an excellent insulator (k ≈ 0.026 W/(m·K)) — trapped air in clothing and building insulation provides warmth.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Explain thermal resistance and its analogy to electrical resistance.  ·  Q4. Two slabs in series — find interface temperature given k₁, k₂, d₁, d₂, T₁, T₂.  ·  Q5. Why are metals good conductors of heat but wood is not?

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Compare thermal conductivities of materials.  ·  Thermal resistance analogy to electrical resistance.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Air gap as insulator: k_air ≈ 0.026 W/(m·K) — double-pane windows use air gap to reduce conduction.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Rate of heat conduction is proportional to: → A  ·  Thermal conductivity of metals is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Thermal Conductivity (k): Material property measuring ability to conduct heat. SI unit: W/(m·K). Metals have high k (silver ~429, copper ~401, aluminum ~237). Insulators have low k (wood ~0.1, air ~0.026).  ·  Temperature Gradient: dQ/dt = -kA(dT/dx) — heat flows from high to low temperature. Negative sign indicates heat flows in direction of decreasing temperature.  ·  Thermal Resistance: R = d/(kA) analogous to electrical resistance. Heat current H = ΔT/R. Series slabs: R_total = ΣRᵢ; same heat current through each.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Thermal conductivity unit: W/(m·K)  ·  Temperature gradient: dT/dx  ·  Isotropic Material: k is same in all directions — true for most polycrystalline materials.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Heat flows from hot to cold.  ·  Believing heat flows from cold to hot: Heat always flows hot → cold spontaneously.  ·  Confusing conduction with convection: Conduction needs no material motion; convection involves fluid motion.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Forgetting steady-state assumption in Fourier's law.  ·  Steady state required — temperature at each point doesn't change with time.  ·  One-dimensional flow assumed — sides insulated.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Thermal resistance concept simplifies composite slab problems.  ·  Temperature drop is proportional to thermal resistance (larger drop across poorer conductor).  ·  Statement 3: Thermal resistance R = d/(kA) — analogous to electrical resistance.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 4: For slabs in series, total thermal resistance is sum of individual resistances.  ·  Statement 5: Metals are good conductors due to free electrons; insulators are poor conductors.  ·  Temperature drop ∝ thermal resistance.
